definitions.definition: That from which the origin, sustenance and dissolution of the world proceed, known from the Upaniṣads (BS 1.1.2–4).
The one reality without a second: existence–consciousness–bliss, attributeless (nirguṇa) in itself, identical with the inner self; associated with māyā it is Īśvara, the world-cause.

equivalents.note: Advaita holds Brahman and the inner self identical; other Vedānta schools deny strict identity.

definitions.definition: The inner self (pratyag-ātman): pure, self-luminous consciousness, the witness of the three states, not the body, senses, mind or ego; identical with Brahman.
The supreme self, i.e. Brahman as the self of all; not different from the inner self.
Existence/being: that which is never sublated in the three times; Brahman as pure being, present in every cognition 'it is'.
Consciousness: self-luminous awareness, the nature of the self and of Brahman, never an object.
Bliss: the nature of Brahman, not a quality it has; worldly joys are fragments of it, manifest in deep sleep as unobstructed bliss.
Being–consciousness–bliss: the three words indicate, by excluding their opposites, the one attributeless Brahman; they are not three attributes.
Without attributes: Brahman in itself, free of all qualities, relations and distinctions (BS 3.2.11, 3.2.14 as read by Śaṅkara).
With attributes: Brahman as associated with māyā — Īśvara, omniscient and omnipotent, object of worship and meditation; real at the empirical level.
The Lord: Brahman associated with māyā (or reflected in it), omniscient ruler, creator, sustainer and dissolver, giver of the fruits of action; his lordship depends on adjuncts of name and form.
The prototype (bimba) consciousness, of which the jīva is the reflection.

The individual self: Brahman appearing as limited, reflected or semblanced through the adjunct of the inner organ (and ignorance); agent, enjoyer and transmigrant only through adjuncts; in truth Brahman.
The reflection of Brahman in avidyā/the inner organ, real and identical with the prototype.
Brahman delimited by the inner organ; the locus of ignorance.
The witness: consciousness that illumines the mind and its modes, the three states and their absence, itself unchanging and never an object.

equivalents.note: The witness of the three states is what the Māṇḍūkya calls the fourth; 'witness' names it in relation to what it witnesses, 'fourth' relative to the three states.

definitions.definition: The immutable, 'anvil-like' consciousness underlying the body and mind, distinct from the reflected consciousness (cidābhāsa); another name for the witness.
The semblance or reflection of consciousness in the intellect, which makes the inner organ appear conscious; together with the kūṭastha it constitutes the jīva.
The fourth: not a fourth state beside waking, dream and sleep but the self that pervades and transcends them, non-dual, peaceful, auspicious; the Lord able to end all sorrow (GK 1.10).
Self-luminous: not requiring another cognition to be revealed; defined by Citsukha as being fit to be called immediate while not being an object of cognition.
Experience/awareness itself, the self as pure self-established consciousness (Iṣṭasiddhi).
The Lord's beginningless, indescribable power, consisting of the three guṇas, known from its effects, by which the one Brahman appears as the world; neither real nor unreal (VC 108–109).
In Vidyāraṇya's usage, prakṛti with pure sattva, the adjunct of Īśvara, as distinct from avidyā with impure sattva, the adjunct of the jīva.

equivalents.note: Identical in the Vivaraṇa and Saṃkṣepaśārīraka usage (one entity under two aspects); distinguished by Vidyāraṇya (pure vs impure sattva).

definitions.definition: Ignorance: in Śaṅkara, superimposition itself (the non-discrimination of self and not-self); in later Advaita, a beginningless, positive, indescribable power that veils Brahman and projects the world, removed by knowledge alone.
One positive ignorance having pure consciousness as its locus and object.
Ignorance residing in the individual selves (many, one per jīva), with Brahman as its object.

equivalents.note: Used interchangeably in Advaita texts (Vedāntasāra prefers ajñāna).

definitions.definition: Ignorance, synonym of avidyā: 'something positive, indescribable as being or non-being, made of the three guṇas, opposed to knowledge' (Vedāntasāra).

Ignorance as a positive entity (not a mere absence of knowledge), held by the Vivaraṇa line and later Advaita, proved by the experience 'I am ignorant'; rejected as un-Śaṅkaran by Satchidanandendra (recent).
Root-ignorance: the beginningless causal ignorance that is the material cause of the world-appearance, as distinct from the particular ignorances (tūlāvidyā) of objects.
The veiling power of ignorance, which hides the self as a small cloud hides the sun from the viewer.
The projecting power of ignorance, which projects the world and the subtle and gross bodies on the self, as ignorance of the rope projects the snake.

Superimposition: 'the appearance, of the nature of memory, of something previously seen in something else' — the mutual superimposition of self and not-self that is the basis of all empirical life, called avidyā.
Substratum: the real on which something unreal is superimposed (the rope for the snake; Brahman for the world).
Apparent transformation: a change in appearance without change in the substance, as the rope appears as a snake; the world is Brahman's vivarta and avidyā's pariṇāma.
Transformation of a cause into an effect (BS 1.4.27).
Real transformation (as milk into curd); Advaita accepts it only for māyā/avidyā in relation to the world, never for Brahman, which undergoes only apparent transformation (vivarta).
Indescribable: not determinable as real (since sublated) nor as unreal (since it appears); the status of māyā, avidyā and their products.

False: what appears but is sublated by knowledge; defined as indescribable, as the counterpositive of absence in its own locus in all three times, as removable by knowledge, or as other than the real (five definitions in the Advaitasiddhi).
Sublation: the cancellation of a cognition by a later one that shows its object never was as it appeared (the snake by the rope-cognition); the criterion of the three levels of reality.
Ultimately real: never sublated — Brahman alone.
Empirically real: valid for all practical dealings and sublated only by knowledge of Brahman — the waking world, Īśvara, scripture and the path.
Apparently real: existing only while perceived and sublated by ordinary waking cognition — dream objects, the rope-snake, shell-silver.
Limiting adjunct: something that makes a thing appear with characteristics not its own without changing it (the red flower near the crystal; the pot delimiting space; body and mind for the self).
Reflection: the jīva (or Īśvara) as the reflection of consciousness in an adjunct, like the sun in water (BS 3.2.18).
The prototype or original of a reflection; in the Vivaraṇa, Īśvara/Brahman as the original of which the jīva is the reflection.
Delimitation: the jīva as consciousness delimited by the inner organ, as space by a pot.
Semblance: the jīva as a mere appearance of consciousness in the intellect (Sureśvara); in BS 2.3.50 'reflection'.
Name and form: the empirical world as distinct from being–shining–dear; the adjuncts through which Brahman appears as many.
'A matter of speech': the Chāndogya's description of modifications as mere names (the clay alone being real), the basis of the non-difference of effect from cause (BS 2.1.14).
Sport: creation is the Lord's play, without need (BS 2.1.33).
Creation undertaken as spontaneous play, like breathing; the account belongs to the empirical realm.
The Advaita theory of error: the illusory object (shell-silver) is neither real nor unreal but indescribable, produced for the moment by ignorance.
The rope–snake: stock illustration of superimposition, sublation and substratum.
Shell–silver: stock illustration of error, superimposition in the form of memory, and of falsity.
Pot-space: space delimited by a pot, stock illustration of the jīva as the one self delimited by bodies (GK 3.3).
'The tenth (man)': illustration of the self overlooked by the counter and recognized immediately through the words 'you are the tenth'.
The doctrine of non-origination: nothing whatever is ever born; creation-teachings are only means; the highest truth of Gauḍapāda.
The doctrine that perception is creation: objects exist only while perceived, as in dream (Prakāśānanda).
The doctrine that creation precedes perception: the empirical world, created by Īśvara, exists whether or not it is perceived (majority Advaita view).
The doctrine that there is only one jīva, other beings being appearances within its ignorance, as figures in a dream.
The doctrine of many jīvas, each with its own ignorance or inner organ, so that one is liberated while others remain bound (Bhāmatī and most Advaitins).
The gross body, made of the quintuplicated elements, seat of experience in waking.
The subtle body of seventeen members — five organs of knowledge, five of action, five prāṇas, mind and intellect — made of unquintuplicated elements; it transmigrates.
The causal body: beginningless, indescribable ignorance, the seed of the other two, experienced in deep sleep; the bliss-sheath.
The five sheaths (food, vital air, mind, intellect, bliss) which seem to cover the self; the self is known by discriminating it from each.
The sheath made of food: the gross body.
The sheath of vital air: the five prāṇas with the five organs of action.
The sheath of mind: mind with the five organs of knowledge, the seat of doubt and desire.
The sheath of intellect: intellect with the organs of knowledge, the agent-ego that transmigrates.
The sheath of bliss: ignorance (the causal body) with its joys experienced in deep sleep and in pleasure; for Śaṅkara a sheath, not Brahman (BSBh 1.1.19).
Waking: the state in which the self, as viśva, experiences gross objects through the senses; empirically real.
Dream: the state in which the self, as taijasa, experiences mental impressions; its creation is 'mere māyā' (BS 3.2.3); the model for the waking world's falsity (GK 2).
Deep sleep: the state in which the self, as prājña, rests in ignorance without objects, experiencing bliss; the memory 'I slept happily, I knew nothing' shows the witness and ignorance.
The self as experiencer of waking, identified with the gross body (microcosmic counterpart of Virāj/Vaiśvānara).
The self as experiencer of dream, identified with the subtle body (counterpart of Hiraṇyagarbha).
The self as experiencer of deep sleep, identified with the causal body (counterpart of Īśvara); bound by cause only (GK 1.11).
The cosmic subtle being: consciousness identified with the aggregate of subtle bodies (sūtrātman), collective counterpart of taijasa.
The cosmic gross being: consciousness identified with the aggregate of gross bodies, collective counterpart of viśva.
The inner controller: Īśvara as the consciousness governing each being from within (BĀU 3.7), the 'starched canvas' of the Citradīpa.

The inner organ, one in substance and fourfold in function — mind (manas, doubting), intellect (buddhi, deciding), memory-store (citta) and ego (ahaṅkāra); the adjunct through which consciousness becomes the knower.
Mind: the inner organ as doubting and deliberating; for the Bhāmatī, when purified by contemplation, the instrument of direct realization.
Intellect: the inner organ as deciding; the seat of the reflected consciousness and of the ego's agency.
The inner organ as remembering and reflecting (in the fourfold Advaita division); in general usage, mind.
The ego, the I-maker: the inner organ as appropriating ('I', 'mine'), the knot of superimposition of consciousness and the insentient.
A mode or modification of the inner organ; in perception it goes out and takes the form of the object; the mode in the form of Brahman removes ignorance.

literal: mode in the form of the undivided

definitions.definition: The mental mode in the form of the partless Brahman arising from the mahāvākya; it destroys ignorance and then subsides, like a clearing-nut in water.

Latent tendency: the impressions of past experience and action that incline the mind; the three vāsanās (world, scripture-learning, body) obstruct knowledge; their destruction is a discipline of the jīvanmukta.
The knot of the heart: the ego-knot binding consciousness and the insentient, cut by knowledge (MU 2.2.8).
The state of no-mind: when, through knowing the truth of the self, the mind ceases to imagine, grasping nothing (GK 3.32).
The desire to know Brahman, i.e. the inquiry into Brahman, with which the Brahma Sūtras open.
The inquiry into Brahman undertaken after acquiring the four means, not after the inquiry into ritual.
The qualified student: purified by prescribed duties and endowed with the four means.
The four preliminaries of a teaching text: qualified student, subject, relation and purpose.
The four means: discrimination of eternal and non-eternal, dispassion toward enjoyments here and hereafter, the six virtues beginning with calm, and longing for liberation.
Discrimination between the eternal and the non-eternal: the firm conviction 'Brahman is real, the world is false' (VC 20); also the discernment of self from not-self.
Dispassion toward the enjoyment of results of action in this world and the next.
The sixfold wealth: calm, self-control, withdrawal, forbearance, faith and concentration.
Calm: resting the mind on its goal, withdrawn from objects (VC); control of the mind (Tattvabodha).
Self-control: restraining the outer organs and turning them back to their sources.
Withdrawal: the mind's not leaning on external things (VC 23); defined by the Tattvabodha as performance of one's own dharma, and by others as renunciation of works.
Forbearance: enduring heat and cold, pleasure and pain and all afflictions without retaliation or lament.
Faith: firm trust in the words of scripture and teacher, by which the truth is grasped.
Concentration: keeping the intellect steadily fixed on Brahman (VC); one-pointedness of mind (Tattvabodha).
Longing for liberation: the desire to be freed from bondage by knowing one's true nature.
Hearing: ascertaining, under a teacher and by the six marks of purport, that the Upaniṣads teach the non-dual Brahman; for the Vivaraṇa the principal means.
Reflection: continual consideration of the teaching by reasoning in accord with it, removing doubts about the object.
Contemplation: the flow of like ideas (of the self as Brahman) excluding unlike ones, removing contrary habitual notions; for the Bhāmatī the principal means.

equivalents.note: Advaita distinguishes nididhyāsana (dwelling on the known truth of the self) from upāsanā (meditation on a supported object, an act enjoined); Maṇḍana and the Bhāmatī bring them closer.

definitions.definition: Inquiry into the self: 'Who am I? How did this world arise? Who is its maker? What is its material?' (Aparokṣānubhūti 12); inquiry, not action, attains the Real (VC 11).
A contemplative exercise in the Upadeśasāhasrī's prose part: reviewing sound and the other objects as not-self and oneself as pure unrelated awareness.

Repeated meditative contemplation of the Upaniṣadic knowledge to make it direct and to destroy the impressions of difference — required by Maṇḍana, rejected as necessary by Śaṅkara (US 18) and Sureśvara.

Meditation/worship: sustained mental activity directed to a prescribed object (the qualified Brahman, a symbol), an act that can be enjoined; purifies and steadies the mind and leads to the Brahma-world.
Meditation on the object as oneself ('I am Brahman'), as opposed to symbol-meditation (BS 4.1.3).
Meditation on Brahman through a symbol (name, mind, sun, Oṃ); the symbol is not to be taken as the self (BS 4.1.4).
A 'consistent error' that nevertheless leads to its object, as taking a gem's light for the gem leads to the gem; used for meditation on the attributeless (Pañcadaśī 9).
Absorption in which the mental mode rests in Brahman while the distinction of knower, knowing and known remains.
Absorption in which the mental mode in the form of Brahman remains, unmanifest, with no distinction of knower and known, like salt dissolved in water; distinct from sleep because the mode persists.
Dullness: the mind's lapse into sleep for want of support, first obstacle to nirvikalpa samādhi.
Distraction: the mind's turning to external things; also the projecting power of ignorance.
Latent attachment: the mind's stiffening under impressions of attachment even without distraction.
Relishing: enjoying the bliss of savikalpa samādhi (or of the calm mind), which prevents going further.
Destruction of latent tendencies, practised with knowledge and mind-dissolution for the stable freedom of the jīvanmukta.
Dissolution of the mind: the mind's ceasing to take on forms, practised by the knower for stable abidance.
'Contactless yoga': Gauḍapāda's discipline of the mind that realizes the unborn, free from contact with objects, feared by yogins who see fear where there is none.
Purification of the mind, the proper result of selfless action, which makes one fit for knowledge.
The desire to know (Brahman), produced (per the Bhāmatī) by sacrifice, gifts and austerity (BĀU 4.4.22).
Renunciation by one who desires knowledge, as a means to it.
Renunciation by the knower, for the stable enjoyment of liberation while living.
The highest class of renunciant, established in knowledge of the self, beyond ritual marks; the model of the vidvat-sannyāsin.
Obligatory daily rites (e.g. sandhyā), whose omission incurs sin; performed without desire they purify the mind.
Desire-prompted rites for particular results (heaven etc.), to be avoided by the seeker.
Liberation, from which there is no return (BS 4.4.22).
Liberation: not produced but the eternal, bodiless nature of the self, realized when ignorance is removed by knowledge; the attainment of bliss and cessation of sorrow.
Liberation while living: the knower remains embodied till prārabdha is exhausted, free of bondage, agency and sorrow.
Bodiless liberation at the fall of the body, when prārabdha is exhausted; nothing is gained that was not already the case.
Gradual liberation: meditators on the qualified Brahman reach the Brahma-world by the path of light and are liberated with its ruler at the end of the cycle (BS 4.3.10).
Immediate liberation of the knower of the attributeless Brahman, whose prāṇas do not depart (contrasted with krama-mukti).
Karma that has begun to bear fruit and produced the present body; not destroyed by knowledge but exhausted by experience, like the momentum of a potter's wheel.
Accumulated karma not yet begun to bear fruit; burnt by knowledge.
Karma done after knowledge, which does not cling to the knower, as water to a lotus leaf.
The path of the gods, beginning with light (arcis), by which meditators go to Brahman/the Brahma-world without return (BS 4.3.1).
The path of the fathers, taken by performers of rites, leading to the moon and return to earth with residual karma (BS 3.1).
The path 'beginning with light': the stations of the path of the gods (BS 4.3.1–6).
The world of the conditioned Brahman (Hiraṇyagarbha), reached by meditators on the qualified Brahman, where they are liberated at the end of the cycle.
Dissolution, fourfold: daily (deep sleep), occasional, elemental, and final (liberation).
Quintuplication: each subtle element is halved, one half divided into four, and each gross element formed of half of itself and an eighth of each of the other four.
Subtle (unquintuplicated) elements arising from Brahman-with-māyā in the order space, air, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1), material of the subtle body.
'The unmanifest' (Kaṭha 1.3.11), which the sūtras deny to be Sāṃkhya's pradhāna (BS 1.4.1); Brahman is also called unmanifest (3.2.23).
A name of māyā, the unmanifest power of the Lord (VC 108).

A 'great saying' of the Upaniṣads teaching the identity of self and Brahman: prajñānaṃ brahma (ṚV/Aitareya), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (Yajur/BĀU), tat tvam asi (Sāma/ChU), ayam ātmā brahma (Atharva/Māṇḍūkya); each is assigned to one of the four āmnāya maṭhas.
'You are that' (ChU 6.8.7): the teaching sentence whose word-meanings, purified by exclusive-non-exclusive implication, indicate the identity of the inner self and Brahman.
'I am Brahman' (BĀU 1.4.10): the realization sentence (anubhava-vākya), mahāvākya of the Yajurveda and of Śṛṅgeri.
'Consciousness is Brahman' (Aitareya 3.3): the defining sentence (lakṣaṇa-vākya), mahāvākya of the Ṛgveda and of Govardhana (Purī).
'This self is Brahman' (Māṇḍūkya 2): the practice sentence (abhyāsa-vākya), mahāvākya of the Atharvaveda and of Jyotirmaṭh.
Implication (secondary signification), used when the direct meaning of words is incompatible; in 'tat tvam asi' the words indicate pure consciousness by implication.
Also: a definition or defining mark (as svarūpa- and taṭastha-lakṣaṇa).

literal: implication that leaves and does not leave

definitions.definition: Exclusive-non-exclusive implication: dropping the incompatible part of each word's meaning and retaining the compatible part, as in 'this is that Devadatta'; applied to 'tat tvam asi'.
Exclusive implication, which abandons the direct meaning entirely (the village 'on the Gaṅgā' = on its bank); rejected for 'tat tvam asi'.
Non-exclusive implication, which retains the direct meaning and adds to it ('the red runs' = the red horse); rejected for 'tat tvam asi'.
Co-reference: two words in the same case referring to one thing, the grammatical relation of 'tat' and 'tvam'.
Partless meaning: a sentence that conveys a single non-relational entity, as the mahāvākya conveys the one self.
'Not so, not so' (BĀU 2.3.6): negating all specifications of Brahman by adjuncts, not Brahman itself (BS 3.2.22).
Deliberate superimposition by scripture and teacher (creation, sheaths, attributes) as a provisional teaching device.
Retraction: showing that what was superimposed is nothing but its substratum, as the snake is only the rope.
Definition by own nature: satyaṃ jñānam anantam / existence–consciousness–bliss.

literal: defining mark standing on the bank

definitions.definition: Incidental definition: Brahman as the cause of the world's origin etc., pointing to it as the crow points out the house.
The six marks of a text's purport — opening and close, repetition, novelty, fruit, praise, demonstration — by which hearing determines that the Upaniṣads teach the non-dual Brahman.

Means of valid knowledge: six in Advaita (perception, inference, comparison, testimony, presumption, non-cognition), all valid empirically and all within the sphere of ignorance; scripture alone reveals Brahman.
Valid cognition: cognition of an object not already known and not contradicted.
Perception: the identity of the consciousnesses delimited by the knower, the mental mode and the object; affirmative, not grasping difference (Maṇḍana).
Comparison: knowing the similarity of a remembered thing to one now perceived (the cow is like the gavaya).
Presumption: knowing what must be so to account for something otherwise inexplicable (fat Devadatta who does not eat by day eats at night).
Non-cognition: the means by which absence is known (a jar's absence on the ground), accepted as a separate means following Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā.
Verbal testimony: the Veda, authorless and reproduced by Īśvara at each creation; the only means of knowing Brahman.
Mediate knowledge: knowing that something is, without its being immediately one's own ('there is a tenth').
Immediate knowledge: knowledge of the self as oneself ('you are the tenth'); for the Vivaraṇa produced by the mahāvākya directly.
Knowledge of Brahman, so called because it loosens and destroys the seeds of saṃsāra and leads to Brahman; secondarily the texts.
The three foundations of Vedānta: the Upaniṣads (śruti), the Bhagavad Gītā (smṛti) and the Brahma Sūtras (nyāya).
A topic-section of the sūtras treated in five steps: subject, doubt, prima facie view, conclusion and connection.
The teacher who is learned in scripture and established in Brahman, through whom alone the knowledge is to be sought (MU 1.2.12); approached with humility, service and questioning.
Learned in the Veda; with brahmaniṣṭha, the double qualification of the teacher.
Established in Brahman: having direct knowledge of the self, the second qualification of the teacher.
One of steady wisdom (Gītā 2.55–72), identified in Advaita with the jīvanmukta, whose wisdom is the non-conceptual mode apprehending the identity of self and Brahman (VC 427).
One of the four cardinal monasteries founded, in the tradition's account, by Śaṅkara, each tied to a Veda, a mahāvākya and a group of Daśanāmī names.
The title of the pontiffs (jagadguru) who head the āmnāya maṭhas in succession to Śaṅkara.
